idiom_name: type descriptor object + reference from each instance + id-keyed registry
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: define one descriptor value per conceptual type holding the data shared by all instances of that type (and behaviour slots where behaviour varies); give every instance a reference to its descriptor plus its own state; put a factory on the descriptor (new_instance()) so allocation and initialisation have exactly one path per type; and keep descriptors in an id-keyed registry populated from external data, treated as the single source of truth. Keep descriptors immutable once registered and derive tuned types as new descriptors. Type identity then lives in data instead of code, so adding a type is a configuration change - at the price that the compiler no longer checks type membership, so the application must validate type data, fail fast on unknown ids, and keep descriptors alive as long as any instance refers to them.
code_sketch:
registry.register_all(load('types/*.json'))        # {id, base_health, attack, ...}
type = registry.find('troll')                       # unknown id -> fail fast
m1 = type.new_instance()                            # shared type data, own state
m2 = type.new_instance()
m1.take_damage(10)
print(m1.type.attack)                               # delegate type-specific requests
pitfalls: Skipping the registry and constructing descriptors ad hoc creates several competing 'troll' types, so instances that should be the same type no longer compare equal.
Putting per-instance state (current health, position) into the descriptor leaks it to every instance of that type.
Descriptors that are freed, reloaded or replaced while instances still point at them leave dangling type references.

Wrong move: exposing every type-level value as a forwarding getter on the typed class -> the typed class's public API balloons into a mirror of the descriptor and every new type field is a code change anyway -> instead give callers the type reference (or a narrow read-only view of it) and forward only the handful of messages instances are asked to answer.

Wrong move: letting tuned variants be authored as full standalone descriptors with no parent/type-inheritance link -> dozens of near-duplicate type objects drift apart and one balance change must be repeated across all of them -> instead add an explicit base-type link on the descriptor (the pattern's own optional inheritance support) or generate variants from a template.

Wrong move: filling descriptor slots with function pointers for every behaviour you might want to vary -> the descriptor silently re-implements a vtable, but without static dispatch, exhaustiveness checking or a flat data layout, and hot loops pay a data-dependent indirect branch per element -> instead keep behaviour chosen from a small fixed enum or strategy set in code and leave only genuinely data-shaped values in the descriptor.
